paper.title: PRIME: Frequency-Aware Unified Pruning and Merging for MoE Compression
paper.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have emerged as an effective paradigm for scaling large language models, yet their massive parameter footprint poses severe memory challenges for deployment. Existing compression methods typically treat expert pruning and merging as disjoint operations and rely on greedy heuristics, often leading to irreversible information loss or representational pollution. In this paper, we propose PRIME, a unified optimization framework for MoE compression via adaptive PRunIng and MErging. PRIME casts the discrete prune-merge assignment step as a global Integer Linear Programming over a frequency-weighted surrogate objective, jointly selecting pruning and merging decisions while accounting for expert usage. We motivate the frequency-aware objective through an error-bound analysis under fixed representative assignments, and show that the formulation favors high-frequency experts as centroids, promoting routing stability. Extensive experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and Qwen3.5-122B-A10B demonstrate that PRIME achieves strong accuracy retention across knowledge, coding, math, and long-context tasks, while serving benchmarks of merged models quantify the memory and throughput benefits of expert compression in vLLM.

paper.title: DoSA: Dots Sparse Attention
paper.abstract: Sparse attention visits few keys, yet finding them can still require scoring every key with every indexer head. We introduce DoSA (Dots Sparse Attention), a lossless method for making this computation conditional while preserving exact token selection. Its central observation is that Top-K selection requires sufficient evidence to reject a candidate, not necessarily its full score. A seed set supplies a lower bound on the winning threshold. Nonnegative head projections and joint residual bounds upper-bound positive contributions, while activation-informed aggregation bounds the magnitude subtracted by negative heads. The certificate directs full scoring toward candidates that remain eligible; exact-score filtering further reduces writeback and selection work. We establish the certificate and its exact-selection conditions, and analyze how geometry and selection margins govern its effectiveness. Our GPU implementation accelerates the complete Indexer by up to 2.74 times over SGLang and 1.69 times over LiteTopK across English, Chinese, and code workloads. End-to-end evaluation on GLM-5.2 and DeepSeek-V3.2 achieves up to 1.94 times and 1.50 times time-to-first-token speedups over the two baselines, respectively.

paper.title: PreSO: Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation
paper.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses a self-teacher conditioned on privileged information to turn the sparse outcome signal of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) into dense token-level supervision. Yet the teacher's advantage may depend on information unavailable to the student at inference, raising a central question: which privileged changes are worth distilling? We use cross-problem recurrence as an empirical cue for potentially reusable guidance. Comparing the representation shifts induced by full solutions and compact hints, we find that hint-induced shifts are more concentrated and directionally consistent across problems, and yield more sustained downstream gains despite revealing less information. Motivated by this association, we propose Privileged Representation Isolation for On-Policy Self-Distillation (PreSO). At the source, PreSO uses compact hints to limit the solution-specific detail entering the privileged shift. At the target, it estimates a leading low-rank subspace from shifts pooled across related problems, projects the privilege-induced correction onto this subspace, and adds it to the student's unprivileged representation to form the representation-level distillation target. The selected subspace serves as an operational proxy for recurring structure, rather than a guaranteed separation of transferable and instance-specific information. On five competition-level mathematics benchmarks, PreSO consistently outperforms strong baselines across Qwen3-1.7B, 4B, and 8B, improving average accuracy over the base model by 6.8, 9.0, and 10.0 points. Beyond peak accuracy, PreSO attains the highest final-checkpoint average at every model scale, with improvements that persist through the end of training.

paper.title: OPMD: On-Policy Mechanism Distillation Beyond Output Supervision
paper.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) improves language-model by supervising a student on prefixes sampled from its own policy, but its supervision remains confined to the output space. Consequently, OPD transfers what a teacher predicts without supervising the intermediate computation that produces those predictions. Simply distilling intermediate representations like representation matching is insufficient since teacher and student representations may differ geometrically, and even well-aligned hidden states need not be usable by the student's subsequent computation. We introduce On-Policy Mechanism Distillation (OPMD), which transfers teacher-derived intermediate computation while explicitly accounting for its compatibility with the student. OPMD first constructs a student-compatible teacher that transforms teacher representations into intermediate states usable by the student's downstream computation, then it internalizes these states from on-policy trajectories. OPMD achieves the highest average accuracy among the evaluated distillation baselines in all three teacher--student settings, and generalizes to multi-teacher distillation and cross-family supervised fine-tuning. Further analyses show that mechanism supervision yields more effective reasoning and meaningfully alters the student's intermediate computation and solution strategies, supporting that it transfers information beyond output supervision alone. Together, these results establish mechanism-level supervision as an effective way to move on-policy distillation beyond output supervision, enabling students to learn inner mechanisms they can use and internalize.

paper.title: KV4-RL: Unlocking Faster Asynchronous Rollouts for RLVR with INT4 KV Cache Quantization
paper.abstract: Asynchronous rollout improves the efficiency of reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) by reducing under-utilization during long-tail generation. Sustained concurrency also concentrates context processing into fewer decode steps, increasing the KV workload per step. We characterize this \emph{KV concentration} and find that KV cache quantization delivers substantially greater acceleration than weight-only and weight-activation quantization in our matched-workload comparisons. However, INT4 KV rollout can degrade learning even with token-level truncated importance sampling (TIS). We propose \emph{KV4-RL}, which combines calibration-free INT4 KV quantization with selective INT8 protection of attention sinks and recent context. Protecting a bounded number of positions reduces sampler mismatch while retaining most of the speedup from INT4. Across 400 iterations of Qwen3-8B-Base GRPO training, KV4-RL achieves $1.80\times$ cumulative rollout speedup and $1.27\times$ cumulative full-iteration speedup over BF16 rollout, reaching $1.97\times$ rollout speedup over the final 50 iterations. Under a common BF16 evaluator, its final six-benchmark mean accuracy is within 0.5 percentage points of BF16-rollout training for both Qwen3-4B-Base and Qwen3-8B-Base.

paper.title: Reward-Aligned Distillation
paper.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but remains computationally expensive and sample inefficient. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense token-level supervision from a stronger teacher, yet standard OPD distills every token regardless of whether the teacher's preference actually improves task reward. Existing token-selection methods rely on proxies such as uncertainty or teacher--student divergence, which need not identify reward-improving supervision. We introduce Reward-Aligned Distillation (RAD), a bilevel framework that weights distillation signals based on their predicted effect on the student's post-update reward. RAD differentiates through a temporary optimizer step to score each token's supervision, then updates the token weights by projected ascent from the initial token weights. The resulting weights can strengthen, suppress, or reverse individual distillation-gradient contributions. At a matched training-response budget, RAD improves mean accuracy on six competition-math benchmarks over the strongest baselines by 6.5 percentage points for Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and 2.5 points for Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507. RAD-Simple, a simplified variant, achieves comparable math accuracy at the same training-response budget. On LiveCodeBench-v6, RAD reaches 54.69\% and 58.67\% pass@1 with Qwen3-1.7B (non-thinking) and OLMo3-7B-Instruct, respectively, exceeding the strongest baselines by 8.7 and 6.4 points. These results support reward-guided weighting of teacher supervision across model families and tasks.

paper.title: Vesta: Queueing-Aware LLM Scheduling for Real-World Workloads
paper.abstract: Agentic applications generate multi-turn sequences of LLM requests, with each new turn extending the context accumulated from prior interactions and tool calls. Prefix caching reuses the KV cache of earlier turns and avoids redundant prefill, but routing every turn to its cache-affine instance can create severe local queues while capacity remains idle elsewhere. Remote KV cache access relaxes this tension, yet migrating execution adds transfer work and is harmful when the cluster is already congested. Thus, deciding where to execute a request requires reasoning jointly about cache locality, queueing, and the current operating point of the cluster. We present Vesta, a queueing-aware scheduler for distributed agentic LLM serving. Vesta assigns each session a stable holder for its authoritative KV cache while independently selecting an executor for every request. Grounded in classical queueing theory, its objective accounts for backlog, reusable prefixes, KV cache transfer, and the queueing externality of additional service demand; it migrates execution to recover idle capacity when beneficial and favors placements that add the least prefill and transfer work as congestion rises. Vesta also migrates reusable prefixes across length buckets to avoid cold starts. On real-world agentic workloads, Vesta improves throughput by 14.0\% and reduces mean TTFT by 57.8\% over the state-of-the-art scheduler in a PD-colocated deployment. In PD-disaggregated deployments, it reduces mean TTFT by up to 18.1\% and P99 TTFT by up to 29.0\% at matched throughput.

paper.title: Accelerating Cross-Model LLM Inference via Attention Map Reuse
paper.abstract: LLM-augmented data workflows often involve multiple heterogeneous models operating over substantial shared context, such as schemas, tool specifications, interaction history, and intermediate results. Although prefix caching can reduce prefilling overhead, existing approaches are largely limited to reuse within the same model because KV states are tightly coupled to model-specific architectures. We present MapFlow, a system for efficient heterogeneous LLM serving via cross-model attention map reuse. Instead of reusing KV states, MapFlow reuses attention maps, which capture token dependency patterns and are more transferable across models. To enable efficient and accurate reuse, we combine partial recomputation with lightweight linear translation across layers and heads. To make attention reuse practical for long contexts, we further introduce block-level sparse compression and a fused retrieval kernel. Experiments show that MapFlow reduces prefilling latency and improves end-to-end serving efficiency while preserving generation quality across heterogeneous model pairs and multi-turn routing workloads. These results suggest that attention maps provide an effective reusable state for heterogeneous LLM serving, especially in prefix-heavy data workflows. Our code is available: https://github.com/PKU-DAIR/MapFlow.

paper.title: E8 Lattice Key Quantization for Low-Bit KV-Cache Compression
paper.abstract: Compressing the key-value (KV) cache is essential for serving long-context large language models (LLMs) under memory constraints. While current scalar quantization methods achieve significant compression, they typically face a quality-fidelity trade-off, either suffering from performance instability at 2-bit precision or necessitating 3-bit keys to maintain model quality. In this work, we demonstrate that a uniform low-bit k2v2 configuration (2-bit keys and 2-bit values) can preserve near-baseline quality by using vector quantization (VQ) based on the $E_8$ lattice for KV keys. We show that structured VQ exploits correlations across adjacent dimensions to achieve signal-to-quantization-noise ratios (SQNR) higher than those of independent scalar quantization at the same key payload rate. To ensure practical utility, we adapt a table-based asymmetric scoring algorithm that avoids explicit codebook dequantization during attention computation and preserves decode-throughput parity with scalar baselines. Across five LLM families, our $E_8$ k2v2 approach yields \textasciitilde$6\times$ KV compression, roughly 20\% smaller than scalar k3v2 (3-bit keys and 2-bit values), while retaining near-baseline long-context perplexity. In our full-suite perplexity evaluation, $E_8$ improves over scalar k3v2 in 80\% of model--dataset--context settings. These results indicate that $E_8$ lattice VQ improves quality per byte while keeping throughput at parity, suggesting that structured key quantization is a useful primitive for KV-compression stacks. Overall, our work provides a low-overhead primitive for expanding the quality-memory frontier in long-context LLM inference.

paper.title: WUSPruner: Second-Moment-Optimal Transforms for Structured Pruning
paper.abstract: Structured pruning is typically formulated as identifying which model dimensions to remove, often within the model's original representation. However, the effect of coordinate deletion fundamentally depends on the basis in which pruning is performed. This raises a more fundamental question: how should the basis be chosen specifically for coordinate deletion? We introduce WUSPruner, a transform-based framework for structured pruning of large language models. We formulate basis selection as a local linear reconstruction problem that directly minimizes the reconstruction loss induced by pruning. Inspired by the second-moment transformation in WUSH, we consider a WUS transform constructed jointly from activation and weight statistics. We show that under positive-definite second moments, WUS transform minimizes the local reconstruction loss over all invertible changes of basis. In the resulting basis, the activation and weight second moments are simultaneously diagonalized and balanced, causing the deletion error to decompose into independent spectral contributions and yielding a principled criterion for coordinate selection. Guided by this result, we develop a scalable pruning method based on blockwise WUS transformations and compact input projections. Experiments on Llama and Qwen models from 8B to 72B parameters show consistent improvements over structured pruning baselines across language modeling, knowledge, commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation benchmarks, while also delivering practical reductions in inference latency and memory usage.

paper.title: GA-SVD: Generation-aware Singular Value Decomposition for LLM Compression
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong generalization across a broad range of reasoning and generation tasks, but their large parameter counts impose substantial memory and computation costs, hindering deployment in practical resource-constrained settings. One-shot low-rank compression is a promising solution since it reduces model size and inference cost effectively. However, existing SVD-based methods primarily target multiple-choice benchmarks and often fail to preserve performance on generation tasks. Moreover, their rank allocation strategies are typically heuristic. We propose GA-SVD, a generation-aware low-rank compression framework for LLMs. First, we introduce Generation-Aware Weight Whitening (GAWW), which leverages gradients from on-policy knowledge distillation to construct whitening transformations aligned with generative behavior. Second, we develop an evolutionary global rank allocation method that searches for effective layer-wise rank allocation under a given global compression ratio. Across extensive experiments on Mistral-7B, Qwen3 series, and Llama-3.3 models, evaluated on both multiple-choice and generative benchmarks, GA-SVD consistently outperforms existing SVD-based baselines and achieves state-of-the-art (SoTA) results. We further demonstrate scalability by applying our method to models with up to 70B parameters.

paper.title: SARATHI: Decoupled Data-Free Probing and Adaptive Reconstruction for Structured LLM Pruning
paper.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) by permanently removing neurons and weight rows, yielding dense, hardware-agnostic speedup. Existing post-training methods couple neuron selection and weight reconstruction through a shared calibration dataset, introducing domain bias and out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. We propose SARATHI, a framework that decouples these two stages. A data-free \emph{NMF Residual Subspace Probe} scores neurons using intrinsic weight geometry, without accessing any calibration data, and carries a formal connection to Robust PCA. \emph{Adaptive OBS} then reconstructs the pruned weights with a localized calibration batch, operating in $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ peak memory per layer and eliminating the global memory bottleneck of coupled methods. A \emph{Bias Shift Compensation} step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise cause perplexity collapse at high sparsity. Experiments across six models from two architecture families (gated and non-gated FFN) at 15--40\% sparsity show that SARATHI achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.

paper.title: Preserving Updates in Low-Bit Recurrent State Quantization
paper.abstract: Linear attention and recurrent models compress past tokens into a fixed-size state that is updated at every step. However, storing these states in high precision incurs substantial memory and bandwidth costs at large batch sizes, motivating low-bit state quantization. Unlike weights and key--value caches, a recurrent state is requantized after every update, so its quantization errors accumulate across steps. Our analysis shows that these errors are highly coherent across steps, so reducing per-step errors alone is insufficient. This coherence arises mainly from small updates that are lost in rounding. To preserve these updates, we intervene both before and at rounding. Before rounding, we propose Low-Rank Bypass (LRB), which accumulates small updates in a compact low-rank buffer and periodically merges its sufficiently large elements into the state. At rounding, we observe that a state element can even move opposite to its update, and such reversals prove particularly harmful. Therefore, we propose Bounded Directional Rounding (BDR), which rounds reversed elements toward their updates without additional storage. Although BDR enlarges the rounding error, it improves the model, suggesting that the direction of an update matters more than its rounding error at a single step. Across Gated DeltaNet, GLA, Mamba2, and RetNet, our training-free method substantially outperforms INT4, while reducing state memory by up to 5.3$\times$ and speeding up decoding by up to 1.9$\times$ relative to FP32 states.

paper.title: Heterogeneous Structured Pruning Under Resource Constraints for Hardware-Efficient Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Training-free pruning removes weights from pretrained large language models to reduce their deployment cost. However, existing approaches typically consider only the total number of retained weights. Consequently, their pruning decisions do not account for how target hardware stores and processes those weights. These methods select a sparsity structure in advance and apply it uniformly to all projections, rather than accounting for how each structure trades pruning error against latency and memory across sublayers. We propose Heterogeneous Structured Pruning (HSP), a hardware-aware pruning framework that combines two components: (i) a heterogeneous search space of dense, unstructured, 2:4, block-sparse, and head / channel (H/C) pruning options and (ii) structure-regularising constraints based on latency and memory models. Our contribution generalises existing importance-based methods: a global solver selects one option per sublayer to minimise proxy pruning loss under a resource budget, thereby assigning each projection a structure and density. We evaluate HSP on OPT and LLaMA models for an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano Super edge device, where it improves the quality-resource frontiers over training-free baselines. A project page and updated links for the related code is maintained at: cameronbarker.me/publications/hsp.

paper.title: Representational Difference Distillation
paper.abstract: Knowledge distillation transfers representational knowledge from a large teacher network to a compact student. Existing relational and contrastive distillation methods treat all samples uniformly, spending equal gradient on well-matched and poorly-matched regions of the representation space alike. We propose Representational Difference Distillation (RDD), which diagnoses where teacher and student representations structurally disagree and concentrates the distillation signal on those regions. RDD uses two asymmetric affinity matrices that capture opposing directions of misalignment: one identifies samples the student incorrectly considers similar, the other identifies teacher relationships the student has yet to learn. These affinities determine which sample pairs the distillation loss aligns and how strongly it corrects each misaligned sample. On CIFAR-100 with resnet32x4 to resnet8x4, RDD reaches 75.58% test accuracy in our runs, on par with CRD (75.45%) and above KD and RKD. We additionally explore curriculum-based and sampling-based variants, finding that weighting the loss is more effective than filtering the data.

paper.title: LoopQuant: Accurate and Efficient Post-Training Quantization for Looped Transformers
paper.abstract: Looped Language Models (LoopLMs) improve parameter efficiency by recursively reusing shared Transformer modules, yet their repeated computation over evolving recurrent states poses new challenges for low-bit deployment. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods, largely designed for feed-forward Transformers, fail to account for cross-loop activation dynamics, heterogeneous loop sensitivity, and recursive error propagation, leading to substantial performance degradation at low precision. To address these challenges, we propose LoopQuant, a loop-aware PTQ framework for accurate and efficient low-bit quantization of LoopLMs. LoopQuant is built on three core components: 1) Cross-Loop Distribution Canonicalization (CLDC) learns a shared quantization-friendly representation across recurrent states while preserving parameter sharing; 2) Interaction-Aware Loop-wise Precision Allocation (ILPA) allocates activation precision under a fixed bit budget by modeling task-level loop sensitivity and cross-loop interactions; and 3) Loop-Conditioned Task Calibration (LCTC) further aligns quantized inference with the low-bit recursive trajectory through lightweight task-space calibration. Extensive experiments across LoopLM architectures demonstrate that LoopQuant consistently outperforms existing low-bit PTQ methods. On Ouro-2.6B, LoopQuant under W4A4 surpasses all W4A8 baselines in performance, while reducing model memory by 65.3% with only 3.4% additional storage overhead over naive INT4 and achieving a 1.7 times decoding speedup over BF16. These results demonstrate a strong balance among accuracy, compression, and inference efficiency, providing a practical and deployment-friendly solution for low-bit LoopLM inference. The code is available at [https://github.com/Kishon-zzx/LoopQuant].

paper.title: FORGE: Procedural Weight Generation for Sparse MoE Inference
paper.abstract: We introduce FORGE (Fast On-chip Rotor Generation for Experts), a procedural weight generation system for Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) inference. Rather than storing and loading every expert weight tensor from HBM, we show how a compact accelerator inside each Streaming Multiprocessor can regenerate them on-the-fly from $O(\log^2 d)$ rotor parameters per projection. Per replaced layer, gigabytes of stored expert weights are approximated with under a megabyte of seeds. This addresses the dual memory bottleneck of autoregressive Sparse MoE decode, where per-expert FFN operations are HBM-bandwidth-bound at small routed-token counts and the aggregate expert footprint forces multi-node Expert Parallelism (EP) with all-to-all traffic. We realize the approach as the Rotor Generation Unit (RGU), a fixed-function datapath that generates FFN weight tiles without competing with Tensor Core execution. With 30% of the MoE FFN layers replaced across five Sparse MoE models, we estimate 1.3-2.8x higher system throughput at matched GPU count and 1.10-1.15x lower per-user decode latency at short context. In exchange, downstream accuracy on three model families falls below that of the same model fine-tuned without rotor replacement, and the replacement ratio controls this tradeoff. FORGE also expands KV cache capacity by 1.2-2.6x. It is agnostic to the bit width at which weights are stored, so it can compose with quantization. The RGU is fully implemented/verified in SystemVerilog at ~0.9% SM area overhead (0.032 mm^2/SM, 7nm).

paper.title: MLAfication: Efficiently Enabling High-Fidelity MLA for Modern LLMs
paper.abstract: Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA) compresses the KV cache into a latent representation, reducing inference memory and bandwidth. Existing MHA2MLA/TransMLA methods do not support QKNorm and require costly recovery on modern LLMs, especially MoE. We present MLAfication, a QKNorm-compatible, parameter-efficient extension of MHA2MLA. It combines calibrated KNorm, parameter-efficient distillation, contribution-aware Partial-RoPE, and activation-aware joint KV initialization. Across MHA and GQA models, including QKNorm- and MoE-equipped variants, MLAfication preserves performance under substantial KV-cache compression, surpasses the current SOTA on commonsense and long-context benchmarks, and extends MLA conversion to modern architectures. On Qwen3-30B-A3B, MLAfication delivers up to $5.35\times$ the serving throughput of BF16 GQA and, combined with 4-bit KV quantization, reduces the KV-cache footprint by $94.73\%$. Our code is available at https://github.com/JT-Ushio/MLAfication.

paper.title: GPU Goldmines: Tunable WebGPU Kernels for Edge LLM Inference
paper.abstract: As demand for LLM inference grows and consumer GPUs grow more capable, edge deployment is becoming increasingly attractive. WebGPU is compelling in this setting because it offers cross-platform portability and browser accessibility. However, these same strengths also make high performance difficult to achieve, as an implementation that performs well in one context may not perform well in another. To address this, we present GPU Goldmines, a framework for specifying, executing, and tuning WebGPU kernels. We instantiate GPU Goldmines with kernels for key LLM building blocks: matrix multiplication, matrix-vector multiplication, and flash attention. We characterize performance across diverse devices, shapes, and browsers, and use the resulting database to accelerate subsequent autotuning and configuration selection. On shapes drawn from Llama and Qwen models, our matrix multiplication kernels outperform ONNX Runtime and llama.cpp WebGPU kernels by 7.0x and 1.41x geometric mean, respectively, and deliver end-to-end improvements of 1.48x in the prefill stage of llama.cpp for chat workloads.

paper.title: JustOPD: On-Policy Distillation from Autoregressive to Diffusion Language Models
paper.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a post-training approach for large language models (LLMs) that enables a student model to learn a teacher model's distribution from sequences sampled from the student's own policy. Despite its promising capability, OPD for diffusion language models (DLMs) remains underexplored and existing studies primarily focuses on DLM-to-DLM distillation. The limited availability of strong teacher DLMs and the flexible generation order of DLMs impose additional technical challenges as well. However, it remains unclear how to effectively distill knowledge from a strong autoregressive language model (ARM) into a weaker DLM, given the mismatch between the left-to-right decoding of ARMs and the flexible decoding order of DLMs. Inspired by Ni et al. (2026), we propose JustOPD, an ARM-to-DLM on-policy distillation method that uses autoregressive rollouts during training to align the student's generation process with the ARM teacher's left-to-right decoding. This alignment enables effective distillation from ARM teachers while preserving the DLM's flexible generation-order capability at inference time. Experiments using Qwen3-14B as the teacher and Dream-7B as the student demonstrate that JustOPD consistently improves mathematical reasoning performance over the base DLM across multiple divergence choices.

paper.title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
paper.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.

paper.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
paper.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.

paper.title: LoOPSD: On-Policy Self-Distillation with Looped Teachers
paper.abstract: On-policy self-distillation improves a model using guidance from the model itself, but it still requires a teacher that provides more useful predictions than the student. Existing approaches obtain such guidance by giving the teacher additional context or instructions. We ask whether it can instead come from changing how the same model uses its own layers. To address this, we introduce LoOPSD, which searches over a model's layer execution order to construct a stronger teacher and distills its advantage into the student. Specifically, we keep the model weights unchanged while searching for layers to repeat, and use the resulting teacher's predictions on student-generated prefixes to guide learning. We then alternate search and distillation, rebuilding the teacher from the updated student in each round so that the student progressively absorbs the gains from alternative layer execution. Experiments on mathematical and logical reasoning tasks show improvements across models. On GSM8K with a 400-token thinking budget, LoOPSD raises Qwen3-1.7B accuracy from 42.30% to 79.61%; subsequent distillation rounds yield further gains beyond the first round. Together, these findings show that by searching layer execution to construct teachers, we can turn a model's additional computation into improved student capabilities, opening a new avenue for self-distillation to derive supervision from the model's own computation.

paper.title: Teach Me After You Learn It: Lookahead Self-Distillation for RLVR
paper.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) has emerged as a popular training paradigm for LLMs, providing dense, token-level supervision by aligning a model's own distribution with the distribution induced by privileged information. However, existing OPSD methods derive supervision solely from privileged information of the same instance, leaving inter-instance supervision largely unexplored. We propose Lookahead Self-Distillation (LEAD), which introduces inter-instance distillation by allowing the teacher to first learn from other on-policy rollouts before teaching the student. LEAD constructs lookahead teachers through virtual RL updates on disjoint subsets of on-policy rollouts, and uses each teacher to provide cross-group token-level supervision for the other subset. To reconcile the complementary yet potentially conflicting signals from OPSD and RLVR, we introduce harmonious modulation, which adaptively modulates the GRPO advantage based on the agreement between the two signals. Extensive experiments on scientific reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks show that LEAD achieves the best in-domain average performance across model scales while maintaining out-of-domain generalization comparable to GRPO.

paper.title: Two For The Price Of One: Curvature-Aware Pruning Preserves Influence Functions Too
paper.abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.

paper.title: SP$^2$ec: Adaptive Self-Speculative Decoding for Vision-Language Models
paper.abstract: Speculative Decoding (SD) has demonstrated its efficacy in accelerating large language model inference, but for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the diverse input modalities make it difficult for a small trained drafter to achieve consistently high throughput. Self-speculative decoding reuses parts of the target model as a drafter which retains the multi-modal capability of the VLMs, yet its efficiency depends on choosing a suitable draft configuration for each prompt. We propose Single-Peak SPeculative decoding (SP$^2$ec), a training-free bandit algorithm that adapts the draft configuration during generation. SP$^2$ec exploits the single-peak throughput pattern observed in existing self-speculative methods, including SWIFT, KnapSpec, SpecVLM, and our simple cosSim. Our algorithmic design explicitly minimizes a novel notion of wall-time regret for each given query, corresponding to the empirical wall-time latency. Theoretical guarantees on the wall-time regret show that SP$^2$ec can exploit the optimal draft configuration, with negligible exploration cost. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B across visual and textual tasks show consistent improvements of up to 11\% over the original self-speculative methods, demonstrating the wide applicability of the proposed SP$^2$ec algorithm.
